title: Kabir's Flowers: A Saint Both Sides Kept
hook: a story of a sheet lifted from a body, and flowers underneath
carry: bhakti asks whom you love, not your birth
tomorrow: Ram or Allah: which name did Kabir call God?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the guru block with two honest voices: the teacher as a god, and follow only the good deeds. Today, a poet two communities kept.

Marigolds at a wedding, roses on a grave, jasmine pinned in someone's hair: flowers show up wherever people mark what matters. One story people tell ends in flowers. When the poet Kabir died, it goes, his followers gathered, Hindus and Muslims both. The Hindus wanted to cremate him. The Muslims wanted to bury him. The argument grew hot. Then someone lifted the sheet. No body. Only flowers. Each side took half, and went home.
screen: `MARIGOLDS, ROSES, JASMINE.` → `TWO COMMUNITIES, ONE BODY.` → `UNDER THE SHEET, FLOWERS.`

segments.voice: That's a legend, and it's told as one. The history underneath is just as striking. Kabir was a weaver in Benares, remembered as raised in a Muslim weaving family. Hindus count him among the sants of bhakti, the path of loving devotion. The sants sang in the everyday speech of the street, and taught that God is reached by love and by the Name, not by birth, caste or a priest's rites. Kabir's songs question empty ritual wherever he saw it, temple and mosque alike, and keep pointing to a God found within, close as the breath. That's why a Muslim weaver's songs are sung in Hindu homes: as the sants taught it, bhakti asks whom you love, not where you were born. And his verses traveled. Some are gathered in the Bijak, treasured by the Kabir Panth. Others sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture of the Sikhs. He's remembered among Muslims too. That's a shared saint: someone more than one community remembers as its own. Taught as history, that doesn't erase real differences, or pretend the two always lived in peace. Look at the flowers again. Nobody blends the two funerals into one. Each side carries its half home, and honors him its own way.
screen: `A LEGEND, TOLD AS ONE.` · `A SANT OF BHAKTI.` · `LOVE, NOT BIRTH.` · then, large: `HALF THE FLOWERS EACH.`

segments.voice: If there's a flower, a spice jar, a cup of tea or a piece of fruit near you, bring it close and breathe in its smell. Let it fill one breath, then another, slowly. A smell doesn't ask who you are before it reaches you; it reaches everyone in the room the same way. If there's nothing nearby, recall the scent of flowers at a gathering you've been to, and stay with it.
Hindu-Muslim shared saints: holy people like Kabir, remembered by more than one community as their own.
For the road: bhakti asks whom you love, not where you were born. Half the flowers each. See you tomorrow.
